title: Primordial black holes challenge assumptions about natural dark matter
excerpt: A quantitative comparison of 12 dark-matter models found that primordial black holes can be as natural as some particle candidates, undermining blanket assumptions about fine-tuning.
content:
A quantitative comparison of 12 dark-matter scenarios found that primordial black holes can be as “natural” as some of the field’s favored particle models, challenging the tendency to treat black-hole dark matter as an exotic and fine-tuned alternative. The peer-reviewed analysis by Stefano Profumo, a physics professor at the University of California, Santa Cruz, assessed how strongly each model’s predicted dark-matter abundance changes when its input parameters are slightly varied. Particle candidates and black-hole formation mechanisms occupied the full range from highly sensitive to comparatively robust.

Dark matter accounts for most of the matter in the universe and influences the formation and motion of galaxies, but it has never been directly detected. That absence has left physicists searching among numerous candidates, including weakly interacting massive particles, or WIMPs, and hypothetical black holes formed shortly after the Big Bang. Because detection has not provided a decisive test, researchers have also used “naturalness” to compare theories. In this context, naturalness means that a model can reproduce the relevant outcome without requiring its parameters to be adjusted to an implausibly narrow range.

Profumo applied the Barbieri-Giudice measure, a quantitative test of parameter sensitivity, to 12 well-studied dark-matter scenarios. The measure asks how much a predicted result changes when an input value is nudged slightly. A model that changes gradually is considered less fine-tuned, while one that changes dramatically may require unusually precise values. The comparison included several varieties of particle dark matter, including WIMPs and a resonant particle model associated with the Higgs boson, as well as primordial-black-hole scenarios involving different formation processes in the early universe, including collapse of domain-wall networks.

The results did not divide cleanly along the boundary between particles and black holes. Models associated with primordial black holes appeared throughout the sensitivity spectrum, with domain-wall-collapse scenarios among the least fine-tuned constructions studied. At the other end, a popular particle scenario involving annihilation through a Higgs-related resonance required one parameter to be fixed within a fraction of a percent. Profumo said the findings undermine the common narrative that primordial black holes are necessarily exotic and highly tuned while particle dark matter is the safe, natural default. “When you actually run the numbers side by side, that story doesn’t hold up,” he said, noting that some black-hole models were about as natural as the most forgiving particle models, some particle models were severely fine-tuned, and others fell between those extremes.

The study does not establish which candidate is correct. Dark matter remains undetected, and neither the comparison nor the naturalness test can determine whether particles or primordial black holes constitute the missing matter. Its narrower conclusion is methodological: fine-tuning belongs to individual, specified models rather than automatically to entire classes of dark matter. As Profumo put it, “The tuning lives in the specific model, not in the kind of dark matter you started with.” The analysis therefore offers a common ruler for comparing distinct proposals while cautioning researchers against using naturalness as a shortcut for dismissing a whole category of possibilities. The paper, “Primordial black hole dark matter: A quantitative parameter sensitivity comparison across formation mechanisms and particle candidates,” was published in Physical Review D on September 10, 2026.
